Newfane.metaDescription: Bats, raccoons, squirrels, and skunks in Newfane, VT — historic homes around the common and West River valley farms. Same-day service — call us today.
Newfane.housing_era: The Windham County seat, a postcard village of historic homes around its common and courthouse, with the village of Williamsville, the settlement of South Newfane, and farmhouses along the West River and Rock River valleys.
Newfane.geographic_features: West River (flows along the eastern side of town toward Brattleboro), Rock River (joins the West River in South Newfane), Williamsville covered bridge area (the bridge and village on the Rock River), Newfane Hill (elevated historic settlement west of the village)

Newfane.wildlife_intro:
Newfane's Greek Revival homes are as attractive to bats and squirrels as they are to visitors — tall attics, old chimneys, and a century of small gaps. Raccoons work the West River farms and village garages, skunks den under the porches of the common's historic homes, and woodchucks work the valley fields. Williamsville and South Newfane add camps and rural homes where porcupines and red squirrels are the winter problem.

Historic homes need careful hands, and our crew proofs Newfane houses by sealing every gap with materials suited to old fabric, fitting bat one-way doors in spring or late August through fall, and finishing in winter when colonies are gone. No colony work happens while pups cannot fly. Fall is also mouse season in these big old houses, so call us early for a full inspection before the cold sets in.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. After an inspection, our crew can explain the options and the cost for your home or camp in Newfane, with no pressure to go ahead.

faqs.q: How do you keep bats out of a historic Newfane home for good?
faqs.a: By treating the whole building, not the one visible entry. Bats use several small gaps, and sealing only the busy one moves them to the next. Our crew seals every other opening, fits one-way doors at the active exits in the right season, and returns to finish the last seals once the colony has left — that sequence is what ends it.

Brattleboro.wildlife_intro:
Brattleboro is southern Vermont's most urban wildlife market. Raccoons and skunks are bold downtown, rats work the restaurant and riverfront blocks, and squirrels and bats occupy the attics of its dense older housing from downtown to West Brattleboro. Opossums are established in the Connecticut River valley and are nightly visitors here, and the West River and Whetstone corridors move animals through town constantly.

Fall brings the usual mouse and squirrel rush, spring brings denning raccoons and skunks, and summer bat colonies in the big old multi-family homes are exclusion only — one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, proofing in winter, and no colony work while pups cannot fly. In dense housing our crew inspects shared rooflines and walls carefully, because one building's gap is often the whole block's problem. Call us early in the season.

faqs.q: Why are opossums so common in Brattleboro?
faqs.a: The Connecticut River valley is prime opossum country in Vermont — milder winters, river food, and plenty of den sites under decks, sheds, and porches. They are established here in a way they are not in the colder Northeast Kingdom. Most pass through, but our crew can remove one that has settled under a building and seal the space.

Porcupines trouble the hill homes toward Putney Mountain.

The valley's seasons are a little gentler, but fall still drives mice and squirrels into Putney's older homes, and our crew proofs them every autumn. faqs.q: Are skunks a particular problem in Putney?

Townshend's valley farms and village homes share a familiar list: bats in farmhouse and barn lofts, raccoons in feed rooms and chimneys, squirrels in the village's older homes, and woodchucks under outbuildings in nearly every field. Skunks den under porches each spring, beavers work the brooks above the lake, and the wooded hills keep porcupines close to camps and rural homes.

Our crew works Townshend on the valley calendar — fall proofing before winter, denning calls in mud season, and bat exclusions in spring or late August through fall with one-way doors. Winter is for sealing empty buildings, and no colony work happens while pups are flightless. A valid Vermont trapping license is required for compensated trapping, and our crew works under one — ask us about the options for your property when you call.

faqs.q: Can beavers be kept from flooding Townshend fields without removing them?
